description: Let's dance to the space groove.
summary: MapSonifier is an “Earth Jukebox” that adds sound to NASA EIC world-map animations, so they can be experienced through hearing as well as sight. You provide two input files: the visualization video (mp4) and its color bar image. The app reads the color bar’s name, unit, value range and scale type (linear, logarithmic or unevenly labelled), then matches the color of every pixel in the video frames to a real measurement. It divides the world map into twelve regions, seven land and five ocean, and plays one voice per region in sync with the video. Low values sound bright, major-key and heavenly. As values rise, the choir fades and particle-detector clicks grow denser, so listeners can hear how each region changes over time. You can mute regions and set what counts as low or high. It is designed to work with any EIC video that has a color bar, such as PM2.5, CO, ozone, NOₓ, temperature, humidity, wind or precipitation, and it runs entirely in a web browser.
details:
MapSonifier is an “Earth Jukebox” that answers NASA’s call to make EIC visualizations accessible beyond sight. These animated maps are conveyed almost entirely visually, which leaves out blind and low-vision users and limits how anyone else can explore the data. MapSonifier turns the same visualization into a live, multi-sensory soundscape.

MapSonifier NASA's EIC video and its color bar image as inputs. It reads the legend’s text (name, unit, labelled values, and whether the scale is linear, logarithmic or unevenly spaced) and converts the video frame's pixel’s color into a real measurement by matching it to the bar. It averages the values over twelve regions - seven lands and five oceans - weighting by latitude and ignoring coastlines and labels, and plays one voice per region in sync with the video. Low values sound bright, major-key and heavenly, while high values fade the choir and add denser particle-detector clicks, so a listener can follow how the planet changes over time and compare regions without seeing the map. Users can mute regions, set what counts as low or high, and reverse the mapping.

It is designed to work with any video and color bar, and reads the legends for PM2.5, CO, ozone, NOₓ, temperature, humidity, wind and precipitation. We chose musicality over raw noise so the sound is pleasant enough to invite repeated listening and an emotional connection to the data.

It is built with HTML, JavaScript, the Web Audio API and the HTML canvas, so it runs offline in a browser with no uploads. Python (OpenCV, NumPy, SciPy), FFmpeg and a headless browser were used for analysis and testing, on an ordinary laptop. The choir uses sampled voices from a General MIDI soundfont (Tim Brechbill, GPL-2). The code was developed with help from Claude (Sonnet 5.5).
